title: Assam Floods Kill 75 as Entire Villages Vanish Across Upper Assam
excerpt: A cloudburst in Nagaland triggered catastrophic flooding across seven districts, displacing over 3 lakh people and submerging more than 45,000 hectares of farmland in what residents call the worst deluge in living memory.
body:
• The death toll from Assam's floods has reached 75, with seven fatalities reported on July 29 in Sivasagar district alone.
  • Over 3.32 lakh people remain affected across seven districts, with 32,477 sheltering in 81 relief camps.
  • The Assam government has raised ex gratia compensation to Rs 9 lakh per victim and announced Rs 15,000 interim relief for the worst-hit families.
  • More than 45,000 hectares of cropland are submerged, threatening the agricultural livelihoods of tens of thousands of families.

At around 7 pm on July 21, floodwaters entered Rohini Duwara's home in Lakwa Abhayapuri village in Assam's Charaideo district. His wife Tutumoni and daughter Bidisha were swept away first. His sons Bidyut and Biplab jumped in to save them but were carried off by the current. Within minutes, Rohini lost three children. The search for Tutumoni continued days later.

Their story is one of dozens playing out across Upper Assam, where a cloudburst in Nagaland's Mon district on July 19 sent the Brahmaputra's south-bank tributaries — the Dikhow, Disang, Janji, and Dhansiri — surging past danger levels. The resulting floods have killed 75 people, displaced more than 700,000, and left residents describing it as the worst deluge in living memory.

Seven Districts Underwater

As of July 29, seven districts — Sivasagar, Charaideo, Golaghat, Jorhat, Nagaon, Sonitpur, and Kamrup Metropolitan — remain under water. The floods have spread across 622 villages and 21 revenue circles, according to state disaster management officials.

Charaideo is the worst-hit district, with 1.42 lakh people affected. Sivasagar follows at 97,074 and Jorhat at 57,371. India Meteorological Department data shows Charaideo received 170 mm of rainfall during the crisis period — 436% above normal. Golaghat recorded 147.9 mm, Jorhat 105.2 mm, and Sivasagar 93.2 mm.

Near Jorhat, satellite imagery showed the Brahmaputra stretching across nearly 21 kilometres — roughly three times its earlier visible spread — engulfing fields, sandbars, and settlements.

Scale of Destruction

In Golaghat district alone, 180 villages and 52,000 families have been affected. Entire neighbourhoods in Kapuhatting, Rajanakhat, Kharjan, and Mahatgaon remain submerged. Most mud houses are uninhabitable even where water levels have slightly receded, with foundations and floors extensively damaged.

"The flood has caused massive damage in our area. Many families have lost their homes, agricultural land, and sources of income. Relief materials have helped us survive, but we need permanent solutions — proper drainage systems and financial assistance to rebuild our lives."

— Dhurbo Das, resident of Golaghat

Across the flood zone, 45,341 hectares of cropland lie underwater. Houses, cow sheds, schools, and anganwadi centres have sustained heavy damage. An estimated 1.39 lakh animals have been affected, and over 500 livestock — including poultry — were reported washed away from a single village in Sivasagar.

Rescue and Relief Operations

The Indian Army, Air Force, NDRF, SDRF, Fire and Emergency Services, and civil volunteers are running continuous rescue operations. Helicopters have been dropping food packets to villages cut off by road. In one operation, a military helicopter flew 13 fishermen stranded for four days on a Brahmaputra island to safety.

Eighty-one relief camps are operational across the affected districts, sheltering 32,477 displaced people, with another 34 distribution centres providing supplies.

"Food packets are dropped from helicopters, but many become wet after falling into floodwaters. Even when food reaches families, they do not have a dry place to keep it or eat it."

— Rajib Kalita, Managing Director, ASHA (Association of Social and Human Activists)

Kalita noted that shelter and drinking water have overtaken food as the most urgent needs. "People keep telling us, 'Do not think only about food. What we need right now is drinking water and shelter too,'" he said.

Government Response

Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has increased the ex gratia compensation for flood victims' families from Rs 4 lakh to Rs 9 lakh — adding Rs 5 lakh from the CM's Relief Fund. The mandatory post-mortem requirement for availing the compensation has been waived; a circle officer's certificate will now suffice. For missing persons whose bodies are not found within a month, the full Rs 9 lakh will be granted.

Families in the four worst-hit districts — Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat — will receive an interim payment of Rs 15,000 for household needs. Students in Sivasagar and Charaideo will receive aid for uniforms and textbooks.

Residents of Golaghat, however, say temporary aid falls short. Locals have urged the Centre to announce a special economic package for the region, requesting Rs 10–12 lakh per affected family. They point to structural issues: the Kuliyapani region's narrow river channels prevent timely drainage, causing flooding year after year.

The Road Ahead

While the affected population has declined from a peak of 4.45 lakh on Monday to 3.32 lakh on Wednesday, the crisis is far from over. Low-lying areas retain water for weeks after the initial surge, and the IMD has forecast more rain, thunderstorms, and lightning across Assam.

"The water will not disappear tomorrow. Even after 10 days, many families will still be displaced. By then, media attention may reduce, but their problems will not," Kalita warned.

For the Indian diaspora from Assam and the Northeast, the floods are a painful reminder of the region's recurring vulnerability. Assam's Brahmaputra Valley, sustained by more than 50 tributaries, faces catastrophic flooding nearly every monsoon season — yet permanent flood control infrastructure remains inadequate, and the cycle of devastation continues.
nri_angle: The devastating Assam floods connect deeply with the Indian diaspora, many of whom have family in the affected Upper Assam districts and are watching the destruction of ancestral villages from abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
